description: Rule catalog shared by the Python (plotnine/matplotlib) and any future R (ggplot2) implementation. IDs are permanent: the third character is the tier; a retired ID is never reused.

retired.LB202: Moved to opt-in Tier 3 as LB301 after calibration (fired on 42% of plots, low precision), 2026-11-20

max_categorical_colors.description: Most categorical colors before a warning

cvd_min_delta_e.description: CIEDE2000 distance below which two colors count as confusable under simulated color-vision deficiency

overplot_min_points.description: Fewest points before overplotting is checked

overplot_fraction.description: Share of points overlapping another at full opacity that counts as overplotting

discrete_points_per_category.description: Points stacked on one category of a discrete axis (without jitter) that counts as overplotting

max_pie_slices.description: Most pie slices before a warning

max_lines.description: Most lines in one panel before a warning

min_font_pt.description: Smallest acceptable text size, in points

min_bars_to_sort.description: Fewest bars before unsorted order is flagged

min_box_group_n.description: Groups with fewer observations than this get flagged in a box plot without points

max_stack_segments.description: Most segments in a stacked bar before a warning

min_mark_contrast.description: Lowest acceptable contrast ratio between data marks and the panel background. WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3.0; the default is lower because most standard palettes (including matplotlib's default orange) fall between 2 and 3.

min_text_contrast.description: Lowest acceptable contrast ratio for normal text (WCAG 1.4.3); large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) needs 3.0.

rules.title: Bar or area axis excludes zero
rules.why: A bar's length encodes its value. When the value axis doesn't start at zero, bar lengths stop being proportional and small differences look large.
rules.fix: Remove the axis limits so the bars start at zero; if the zoomed view matters, show the values as points or a line instead of bars.

rules.title: Dual y-axes
rules.why: Two independent scales on one panel make the crossing points and relative slopes arbitrary: rescale either axis and the story changes.
rules.fix: Use two panels that share the x-axis, or index both series to a common baseline.

rules.title: Log scale silently drops data
rules.why: Zero and negative values have no logarithm. They vanish from a log axis with at most a console warning, so the chart quietly shows less data than the reader assumes.
rules.fix: Use a pseudo-log or symlog transform, or filter the values out and say so in the caption.

rules.title: Rainbow colormap for ordered data
rules.why: Rainbow colormaps aren't perceptually ordered: brightness jumps create false boundaries, and they fail for readers with color-vision deficiency.
rules.fix: Use `viridis` or `cividis` for sequential data; a diverging map such as `RdBu` centered at the midpoint for data with a meaningful center.

rules.title: Too many categorical colors
rules.why: Readers can reliably match only about eight hues to a legend; beyond that, colors repeat or become too similar to tell apart.
rules.fix: Highlight the few categories that matter and gray the rest, facet, or label directly.
chartability: Meaningful elements can be distinguished from each other

rules.title: Quantitative axis has no label
rules.why: Without a label the reader can't tell what is measured or in what units.
rules.fix: Add an axis label with units.
chartability: Axis labels are unclear or missing

rules.title: Overlapping tick labels
rules.why: Overlapping labels can't be read, so the axis stops doing its job.
rules.fix: Swap axes first (`coord_flip()` / `barh`); then fewer ticks or shorter labels. Rotation isn't a fix (see AX202).

rules.title: Legend covers data
rules.why: A legend drawn over the data hides exactly the marks the reader is trying to see.
rules.fix: Place the legend outside the plotting area, or label the series directly.
chartability: Meaningful elements can be distinguished from each other

rules.title: Low-contrast text
rules.why: Text that is too close in brightness to its background can't be read by people with low vision, on a projector, or in sunlight. WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
rules.fix: Darken the text (or lighten the background) until it meets 4.5:1.

rules.title: Overplotting
rules.why: When many points land on top of each other, density becomes invisible: a thousand points in one spot look the same as one.
rules.fix: Add transparency, jitter discrete positions, bin the points (2D histogram / hexbin), or sample.

rules.title: 3D for 2D data
rules.why: Perspective distorts length and area, and bars hide behind each other; the third dimension adds no information.
rules.fix: Use 2D bars, grouped bars, or a heatmap.

rules.title: Line connects unordered categories
rules.why: A line implies continuity and order between neighboring points. Between nominal categories there is none, so the slopes mean nothing.
rules.fix: Use points, bars, or a dot plot; keep lines for ordered or time data.

rules.title: Unsorted bars on a nominal axis
rules.why: With nominal categories, the reader's question is usually 'which is biggest?'. Alphabetical order hides the ranking and makes the reader do the sorting.
rules.fix: Order the bars by value; suppress this rule when the category order is meaningful.

rules.title: Rotated or crowded category labels
rules.why: Tilted text is slow to read, even at 30°. Rotating labels usually means the axes should be swapped so long category names read horizontally.
rules.fix: Swap the axes (`coord_flip()` / `barh`). Time axes stay horizontal: use fewer ticks or a shorter date format.

rules.title: Free facet scales
rules.why: Panels side by side invite comparison. With free scales, the same bar height or slope means different values in different panels.
rules.fix: Use shared scales, or say in the title or caption that each panel has its own scale.

rules.title: Default histogram bins
rules.why: A histogram's shape depends on its bins. The library default is arbitrary, so patterns can appear or vanish depending on a choice nobody made.
rules.fix: Choose a bin width that means something in the data's units.

rules.title: Ordered categories in alphabetical order
rules.why: Months, weekdays and rating scales have a natural order. Stored as plain strings, they sort alphabetically (Apr, Aug, Dec...), which scrambles the pattern the chart should show.
rules.fix: Make the column an ordered Categorical in its natural order.

rules.title: Log values on a linear axis
rules.why: Plotting log-transformed values on a linear axis makes readers decode logarithms (what is 4.7?). A log-scaled axis keeps the original units on the ticks.
rules.fix: Plot the original values on a log-scaled axis instead.

rules.title: Fractional ticks on whole-number data
rules.why: Ticks like 2017.5 on years, or 2.5 on a count of people, label values the data can't take and make the chart look careless.
rules.fix: Put ticks on whole numbers only.

rules.title: Colors indistinguishable with color-vision deficiency
rules.why: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a color-vision deficiency, most often red-green. Categories that differ only by such colors merge for them.
rules.fix: Use a CVD-safe palette such as Okabe-Ito, or add a second encoding (shape, linetype, direct labels).

rules.title: Diverging data on a sequential color scale
rules.why: When values run from negative to positive (correlations, changes, residuals), zero is the meaningful middle. A sequential scale gives zero no special color, so readers can't tell positive from negative at a glance.
rules.fix: Use a diverging colormap centered at zero, e.g. RdBu with vmin = -vmax.

rules.title: Color that encodes nothing
rules.why: Giving every bar its own color invites readers to look for a meaning that isn't there, and it uses up color you may need for something that matters.
rules.fix: Use one color for all bars, and save color for a variable or a highlight.

rules.title: Low-contrast marks
rules.why: Lines, points and bars that barely differ from the background (pale yellow on white, light gray on gray) disappear for readers with low vision and on projectors. WCAG asks for 3:1 contrast for graphics needed to understand a chart.
rules.fix: Use a darker color for the marks, or give light fills a dark outline.

rules.title: Label is a raw variable name
rules.why: Column names are code: `avg_income_usd` is how a program refers to the data, not how a reader does. plotnine and pandas use the column name as the label unless you change it.
rules.fix: Write a label for people: words, capitalized, with units.
chartability: Axis labels are unclear or missing

rules.title: Redundant legend
rules.why: When color repeats what an axis already shows, or a legend has a single entry, the legend adds nothing but asks the reader to look it up anyway.
rules.fix: Hide the legend, or drop the redundant color mapping.

rules.title: Label doesn't match the values
rules.why: A label that promises percentages over values between 0 and 1, or a proportion over raw counts, tells the reader the wrong scale.
rules.fix: Make the label and the values agree: convert the values or reword the label.
chartability: Axis labels are unclear or missing

rules.title: Scientific offset on an axis
rules.why: An offset like '1e8' in the corner of the axis is easy to miss, so readers misread every tick by orders of magnitude.
rules.fix: Rescale the values (e.g. to millions) and say so in the axis label, or format the ticks in full.
chartability: Data in text is not human-readable

rules.title: Text too small at final size
rules.why: Small text becomes unreadable once the figure lands in slides, a report or a phone screen.
rules.fix: Increase the base font size, or make the figure smaller so text is relatively larger.

rules.title: Legend order doesn't match line order
rules.why: When the top legend entry isn't the top line, readers hunt back and forth between lines and legend to match them up.
rules.fix: Order the legend by each line's last value, or label the line ends directly.

rules.title: Pie with many slices
rules.why: People compare angles and areas poorly; past a few slices, a pie can't show which parts are bigger.
rules.fix: Use a sorted bar chart.

rules.title: Spaghetti lines
rules.why: Past about seven lines, lines tangle and colors can't be matched to the legend.
rules.fix: Highlight the few lines that matter and gray the rest, or facet.

rules.title: Summary bars without uncertainty
rules.why: A bar of means hides spread and sample size: two groups with the same mean can differ wildly in their data.
rules.fix: Add error bars or the raw points, or use a box or strip plot.

rules.title: Box plot hides small groups
rules.why: A box plot summarizes a distribution with five numbers. With only a handful of observations those numbers are unstable, and the box hides how few points there are.
rules.fix: Show the points (jittered) on top of the box, or instead of it, and report n per group.

rules.title: Stacked bars with many segments
rules.why: Only the bottom segment of a stacked bar shares a baseline. With many segments, the middle ones can't be compared across bars.
rules.fix: Use grouped (dodged) bars or small multiples, or keep stacking to the few segments that matter.

rules.title: Color is the only cue
rules.why: Charts get printed in grayscale and read by people with low vision. If categories differ only in hue and have the same lightness, they become indistinguishable (WCAG: don't rely on color alone).
rules.fix: Add a second cue: shape or linetype for the same variable, or label the categories directly.
chartability: Color is used alone to communicate meaning

rules.title: Quantitative label has no units
rules.why: A number without units can't be interpreted: is that dollars or thousands of dollars, seconds or minutes?
rules.fix: Add units in parentheses, e.g. 'Median income (USD)'.
chartability: Axis labels are unclear or missing

rules.title: No title
rules.why: A figure that travels without its surrounding text (a slide, a report, a screenshot) needs its own context.
rules.fix: Add a title; a takeaway title states what the reader should see.

rules.title: Direct labels would beat a legend
rules.why: With a few lines, labeling each line end removes the back-and-forth between lines and legend.
rules.fix: Label line ends and drop the legend.

rules.title: Same category, different colors across figures
rules.why: Readers carry color meaning from one figure to the next. If 'West' is orange in one chart and blue in the next, they'll misread the second.
rules.fix: Define one palette per variable (a dict of category to color) and reuse it in every figure.
chartability: Design is not consistent and familiar

rules.title: Inconsistent themes across figures
rules.why: Figures in one report read as a set. Switching themes or base font sizes between them looks unfinished and makes comparisons harder.
rules.fix: Set the theme and font size once at the top of the notebook.
chartability: Design is not consistent and familiar

rules.title: Excess precision in tick labels
rules.why: Extra decimals add clutter without information.
rules.fix: Format ticks to the precision the step needs.
chartability: Data in text is not human-readable

accessibility.description: Rules tied to Chartability tests and WCAG success criteria, at their published thresholds (marks 3:1, text at least 9 pt).

chartability.citation: Elavsky, Bennett & Moritz (2022). How accessible is my visualization? Evaluating visualization accessibility with Chartability. Computer Graphics Forum 41(3).
